description_full: Gentex Corporation designs, develops, manufactures, markets, and supplies digital vision, connected car, dimmable glass, fire protection technologies, audio products, medical devices, and consumer electronics. It operates through Automotive Products, Audio Products, and Other segments. The company offers automotive products, including interior and exterior electrochromic automatic-dimming rearview mirrors, automotive electronics, and non-automatic-dimming rearview mirrors for automotive passenger cars, light trucks, pick-up trucks, sport utility vehicles, and vans for original equipment manufacturers, automotive suppliers, and various aftermarket and accessory customers; and HomeLink modules for the automotive industry. It also provides variable dimmable windows to aircraft manufacturers and airline operators. In addition, the company offers photoelectric smoke detectors and alarms, visual signaling alarms, photoelectric smoke alarms, electrochemical carbon monoxide alarms and detectors, audible and visual signaling appliances, and bells and speakers used in fire detection systems in office buildings, hotels, and other commercial and residential buildings. It sells its fire protection products directly, as well as through sales managers and manufacturer representative organizations to fire protection and security product distributors, electrical wholesale houses, and original equipment manufacturers of fire protection systems. Further, the company is involved in the research and development of nanofiber chemical sensing products; and market and sale of eSight smart glasses to consumers with visual impairment or eye conditions, as well as of identity authentication and access control products that utilizes biometrics technology. It operates in the United States, China, Germany, Japan, Mexico, South Korea, and internationally. Gentex Corporation was incorporated in 1974 and is headquartered in Zeeland, Michigan.

financial_summary: Gentex Corporation is a mid-cap consumer cyclical business with a $3.9B market cap on $2.5B of annual revenue.
The top line has compounded at +10% over the past three years and +5% annually across the full decade, a respectable pace for a business of this size.
Returns on capital run at 18% against a 9% cost of capital — a 10-point spread that is the clearest signature of an economic moat, with gross margins sitting at 36%.

The business throws off $458M in free cash flow — roughly 18 cents on every revenue dollar, which is the owner-earnings figure that actually belongs to shareholders, and cash conversion sits at 1.53× so those profits are backed by real cash.
On the balance sheet, the balance sheet carries net cash, which is the gold standard: the business never has to make desperate decisions in a bad year.

Management returns a meaningful 10.3% of market cap to owners through dividends and buybacks, a strong signal of disciplined capital allocation, and insider ownership is negligible, so management has little personal stake in the long-term outcome, and within its sector the business captures 2.4× its fair share of profits, a structural advantage visible in the numbers.

sect: Its 19% operating margin runs 11pp above the Consumer Cyclical median (7%), a real cost or pricing edge over peers.
It captures 2.36x its revenue share in sector profits, taking a disproportionate slice of the profit pool.
Over five years it has been losing share of the sector profit pool (-10.8% a year).
The sector is fragmented and competitive (HHI 0.03 across 377 companies in the universe; the top four hold 26% of revenue), so pricing power is hard to come by.
mkt: The shares have drifted lower, down 8% over the past year excluding the latest month.
The price sits near the bottom of its 52-week range, 27% below the high.
With annualised volatility of 26% and a beta of 0.79, it is more defensive than the market.
About $52.4M trades a day, enough to build a position.
In past sell-offs it fell 36% in the 2020 crash, 33% in the 2022 bear market and 65% in 2008.
val: The stock trades 42% below its DCF fair value of $33.39, a meaningful margin of safety.
The fair-value models disagree (dispersion 45%), and the Monte Carlo range runs $27.44 to $41.17 (P10-P90), so treat the estimate as noisy.
On multiples it looks cheap against Consumer Cyclical peers: P/E 10.3 vs 18.8, EV/EBITDA 6.5 vs 10.7 and P/FCF 8.6 vs 16.7 (sector median).
Against its own history it is cheap: the EBIT multiple sits 27% below its 10-year median.
Earnings yields are attractive: an FCF yield of 11.6% (above the risk-free rate) and an EBIT/EV of 12.3% (vs the 8% bar).
The 9 covering analysts target $25.28 on average, 32% above the price.
prof: ROIC of 18% clears the cost of capital of 8.6% by 10pp, the mark of a value creator; returns have been steady (CV 0.18).
It runs a 36% gross margin and converts 18% of revenue into free cash flow.
Earnings quality looks solid: cash conversion of 1.53x.
ROE of 15% comes mostly from margins and asset turnover rather than leverage (1.2x equity multiplier).
It spends 8.0% of revenue on R&D and 1.4% on stock compensation.
hlth: The balance sheet carries net cash of $143.5M.
No distress or manipulation flags (Altman Z 7.8, in the safe zone).
growth: Revenue has compounded at 9.7% over 3 years, 8.5% over 5 years and 5.1% over 10 years.
Net reinvestment is nil (capex and working capital no more than cover depreciation), so fundamental growth is near zero.
Free cash flow has compounded 2.1% a year over five years, short of the 5% durability bar.
Capex roughly matches depreciation (1.2x, 5.1% of sales), a maintenance pace.
Its Rule of 40 score is 25, below the 40 that marks a healthy growth business.
It has beaten earnings estimates by 4.2% on average.
own: Insiders hold little stock (0.5%), and reported institutional holdings exceed 100% of shares (a sign of heavy share lending).
Insiders have only sold over the past year (10 sales, net $1.4M sold).
It returns 10.3% a year to shareholders (7.6% in buybacks and 2.5% in dividends).
The share count has shrunk 2.4% a year over five years, steadily raising each holder's stake.
It has paid a dividend for 22 consecutive years, though it has been cut 1.8% a year over the last five.
people: With about 6,398 employees, each generates about $396K of revenue, in line with the Consumer Cyclical median, and revenue has grown 7.8% a year across its filed history.
That works out to $72K of free cash flow per employee.
CEO pay is $2.2M (6x revenue per employee).
